opus-5.5.text:
I think about it as a division of labor based on what each side is actually good at, rather than splitting it by volume.

The data we collect ourselves is the core data: the data that defines what the model should be able to do. That covers the new task categories, the new embodiments, and the cases where we're still figuring out the right collection protocol. At that stage the process itself is still changing. We're adjusting how operators teleoperate, what sensors we record, how we segment episodes, and what counts as a success. If you hand that to partners too early, you get a lot of data collected under inconsistent assumptions, and cleaning it up costs more than collecting it yourself would have. So our own team stays close to the frontier, where the methodology isn't settled yet.

Once a protocol is stable and we know a certain kind of data reliably improves the model, scaling becomes the main problem. That's where ecosystem partners are very valuable. They have real deployment sites, different environments, different objects, different lighting and layouts, and that diversity is very hard to recreate in our own lab. Partners collecting in factories, warehouses, homes, or retail spaces give us coverage of the long tail that we would never think to stage ourselves.

The key is that we don't just receive data from partners. We try to give them a complete toolchain: standardized collection hardware or specifications, annotation formats, quality checks, and feedback on which data actually helped. If a partner can see that their data made the model better on their own scenarios, they're motivated to keep collecting good data. It becomes a loop rather than a one-off transaction.

So in short, our team does the exploratory, high-precision, protocol-defining collection, and partners do the scaled, diverse, deployment-grounded collection. Over time, things that start in-house move outward to the ecosystem once they're mature, and our own team moves on to the next unsolved capability.

r001.rationale: The response cites partners’ diverse deployment environments, objects, lighting, and layouts, but does not identify diversity of robot configurations as a reason to involve them.

r002.rationale: It says the in-house team handles frontier work, new task categories and embodiments, and unsolved collection protocols, retaining collection for difficult, exploratory work.

r003.rationale: It describes the team refining collection procedures while they are still changing, then involving partners after a protocol is stable.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of it less as a division of labor and more as a question of what each side is structurally good at. Partners in the ecosystem, the people actually deploying robots in warehouses or factories or homes, they sit on the long tail. They see thousands of edge cases we would never think to script in a lab. So for breadth, for coverage of the real distribution of tasks, we lean on them. That data is messy, the annotation is uneven, but it's real, and you cannot synthesize "real" no matter how good your simulator is.

Our own team does something different. We collect what I'd call high-density data. Carefully designed tasks, consistent sensor setups, dense labels, multiple demonstrations of the same behavior under controlled variation. That's the data we use to actually understand what the model is learning, to run ablations, to figure out whether a failure is a data problem or an architecture problem. You can't do that kind of science on partner data because you don't control the variables.

The mistake I see people make is trying to get partners to collect the clean, controlled data. It doesn't work. Their incentive is to run their operation, not to serve your research agenda. So we design the interface so that giving us data is nearly free for them, it falls out of normal operation, and we accept whatever quality that produces. Then we invest internally in the expensive, deliberate collection that nobody else will do.

The last piece is feedback. When the model fails at a partner site, that failure tells us where our internal collection should go next. So the two loops are coupled. Partners tell us where the gaps are, and our team fills them in a way that's actually learnable.

r001.rationale: The response cites partners’ access to real-world tasks and edge cases, but does not identify diversity in robot configurations as the reason.

r002.rationale: It says the team collects controlled, high-density data and fills gaps, but does not state that in-house collection is retained for difficult tasks.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe staff developing collection procedures and then passing them to partners; it describes partners contributing data from normal operations.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between the data we can define clearly and the data we’re still learning how to collect. If a task is well specified, with a clear collection protocol and quality standard, ecosystem partners can help us scale it. But when we’re exploring a new capability or trying to understand why a model fails, our own team needs to stay close to the collection process.

That internal work gives us a feedback loop: collect data, train the model, evaluate it, and figure out what’s missing. Once we understand what makes the data useful, we can turn that into a process partners can reproduce.

So I wouldn’t think of it as a fixed percentage. The division changes as the work matures. We need enough internal collection to know what to ask for and how to judge quality, and strong partners to scale the things we understand.

r001.rationale: The response says partners can scale well-specified data collection, but does not identify diversity of robot configurations as a reason to involve them in establishing the data system.

r002.rationale: It says the team should keep its own collection process close when exploring new capabilities or investigating model failures, communicating in-house collection for difficult, less-understood work.

r003.rationale: It describes internal collection and model evaluation to learn what makes data useful, then turning that understanding into a process partners can reproduce.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it in terms of breadth and depth. Ecosystem partners can help us collect data across a broader range of environments and tasks. Our own team should focus on the data where we need very tight control—how the task is defined, how the robot is operated, and how we evaluate the result.

The key is to keep that division connected to what the model actually needs. If we see a particular failure mode, we want to collect targeted data, train on it, and check whether it improves performance. Once we understand what works, we can give partners a clearer collection protocol and scale it up. So it’s a feedback loop, rather than a fixed percentage we assign to each side.

r001.rationale: It says partners can broaden environment and task coverage, but does not identify diversity of robot configurations or establishing the data system.

r002.rationale: It assigns the in-house team tightly controlled data collection, but does not state that the team collects data for difficult tasks.

r003.rationale: It says the team can give partners clearer collection protocols after learning what works, but does not state that staff first work out the data-collection procedures before passing them on.
